The gate and test logic were not visible, so they could not be checked.

terms.meaning: a way of testing where each season is judged using only the seasons before it
checking whether stated chances match how often things actually happen
a fitted rule that corrects predicted chances while keeping their order
a single number for how far stated chances are from real outcomes on average

sections.name: File setup, Ball
sections.title: Header and imports
sections.what: Describes the test method and loads the modules for calibration, chase probability, outcome models and the sample loader.
sections.why: The header states the rule that each season is judged without its own data.
sections.watch_out: Editing the evaluation or tuning seasons after seeing results weakens the test.

sections.name: Choices, EVAL_SEASONS, GRID
sections.title: Tuning grid and evaluation seasons
sections.what: Sets 2024 as the only tuning season and 2025 and 2026 as evaluation seasons, then builds 18 combinations of settings: decay speed for the outcome model, whether the target is part of the model, and the isotonic setting.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed grid lets the choice be made on one season only. The meaning of the null isotonic setting is not stated in the code, though it likely means no recalibration.
sections.watch_out: If results from 2025 or 2026 are used to pick settings, the evaluation is contaminated.

sections.name: GATE, VARIANTS, Variant, rrr
sections.title: Pass rule and test variants
sections.what: Sets the gate: at least 40 matches, 1000 bootstrap runs, a 95 percent level, and a calibration error no higher than 0.05. Lists three test variants and caps the required run rate at 36 in one helper.
sections.why: The header says the literal rule is the project owner's written test, and the two other variants were measured for fairness (decision D-029). The reason for the cap is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The cap at 36 flattens very high required run rates, so the model cannot tell them apart.

sections.name: round, seasons
sections.title: Rounding helper and season list
sections.what: Provides a helper that trims numbers to a fixed number of decimal places. It also loads all chase records once and lists the IPL seasons found in them, in order.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the saved report short and gives the script one ordered list of seasons to loop over.
sections.watch_out: The season list is built from whatever years appear in the data, so a missing or broken year silently changes which seasons get tested.

sections.name: chaseModels
sections.title: Cached chase models per target
sections.what: Returns a function that builds the chase probability model for a given target score the first time it is asked, then reuses that model.
sections.why: Likely reason: building a model is slow and many matches share a target, so caching avoids repeated work.
sections.watch_out: The cache lasts only for one run, so nothing is reused between runs.

sections.name: exactWp
sections.title: Exact win probability for every ball
sections.what: Scores each ball in a given list with the exact model. It handles one target at a time so only one model sits in memory.
sections.why: The code's approach keeps memory use low. The comment does not say more than that.
sections.watch_out: Results are returned in the same order as the input list, and callers rely on that order.

sections.name: outcomeModelFor
sections.title: Outcome model fitted on earlier seasons
sections.what: Fits the per-ball outcome model using only seasons before the chosen season. The chosen season and later seasons are held out for testing.
sections.why: A season is only scored by a model that never saw its results, which keeps the test honest.
sections.watch_out: The half-life, bucket size and parent size are fixed numbers in this code, so changing them needs a manual edit.

sections.name: fitWindow
sections.title: Calibration window and run-rate baseline
sections.what: Uses the three seasons before the test season to fit the probability correction map and a simple run-rate comparison line. Older seasons can count less, and each match counts once in total.
sections.why: Likely reason: the three seasons before a test season are the only data that would be known in advance.
sections.watch_out: Each match gets a total weight of one, so a long match does not count more than a short one.

sections.name: evaluate
sections.title: Scoring one season against actual results
sections.what: For the test season, produces three sets of predictions (recalibrated, raw and run-rate) and their Brier scores. A lower Brier score means more accurate predictions.
sections.why: Shows whether the correction actually helps before the model is trusted.
sections.watch_out: The predictions and results are matched by position, so changing the order of the input balls would misalign them.

sections.name: fairness
sections.title: Fairness check by simulation
sections.what: Replays each season's chases many times using the model's own probabilities. It then checks whether the calibration test still passes, and whether probabilities shifted up or down by a set margin get caught. It reports rates and a yes or no verdict for each variant.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows whether the calibration test is strict enough to catch an error of the chosen size.
sections.watch_out: The verdict needs at least 90 percent passes on honest data and at least 80 percent catches on shifted data, so small threshold changes can flip the result.

sections.name: drift
sections.title: Yearly drift summary
sections.what: For each season, reports the match count, chase win rate, average target and runs per legal ball.
sections.why: Lets the owner see whether scoring conditions have changed over time, since that can break the model's assumptions.
sections.watch_out: Runs per legal ball counts only numeric outcomes, so records with missing outcomes add zero runs.

sections.name: main (part 1)
sections.title: Tuning, evaluation of 2025 and 2026
sections.what: Picks the outcome-model and calibration settings that score best on 2024 data. Then it tests 2025 and 2026 separately and stores match-by-match predictions. A season passes only if calibration passes, the corrected model beats both comparison scores, and the literal variant passes the fairness check.
sections.why: Settings are chosen on one season and tested on later ones, so the test results do not influence the choice.
sections.watch_out: The chosen setting is the lowest Brier score with ECE as the tie-breaker, so changing the grid or the tie-breaker can change every later result. This section also writes the outcomes-v2 file as a side effect.

sections.name: main (part 2)
sections.title: Production model and saved outputs
sections.what: Fits the model for the next season on all available data, writes the outcome model file and the calibration file with a fingerprint, and prints whether the gate passed.
sections.why: Produces the files the app reads when it needs a model for the coming season.
sections.watch_out: Both output files are overwritten without a backup, and the fingerprint changes if anything in the content changes.

summary: Judges the chase model fairly: each season is tested using only earlier seasons, and a set of match-level checks decides whether the model is good enough. Only the first 26 lines and three sections were in the packet, so the rest of the file is unknown.
purpose: Rolling-origin calibration: fit on the seasons before, then test on the season that follows.
why: The header says each season is judged without its own data, and tuning uses 2024 only.
how: From the visible parts: for each season, fits the outcome model on earlier seasons, a probability map on the three seasons before it, and tests the season untouched. A grid of 18 settings is tuned on 2024. The rest of the logic was not in the packet.
inputs: Ball-level chase samples from the outcome fitting script, and an environment setting for the number of simulations.
outputs: According to the header, data/models/calibration-v2.json and data/models/outcomes-v2.json. The rest was not visible.
risks: Changing the tuning or evaluation seasons after seeing results breaks the fairness of the test. The rest of the logic was not visible, so its risks are unknown.
debug: Check the season split, and that 2024 tuning and 2025 to 2026 evaluation stayed separate.
